articles.title: UK diesel price hits all-time high, the RAC says
articles.summary: The US-Israel war with Iran has caused fuel prices to soar due to disruption of global oil supplies.
articles.body:
Diesel prices have hit an all-time high of 199.18p per litre, according to the RAC motoring organisation, as the war in the Middle East continues to push up the cost of fuel.

Petrol prices are also still rising, with a litre currently costing 174.13p.

Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil across the region, causing the price of fuels made from oil to surge.

The RAC said diesel prices had entered "uncharted territory" and served as a reminder of "just how exposed the UK is to events occurring far away".

The cost of diesel has now risen by 59p a litre, or just under 40%, since the US-Israel conflict with Iran erupted at the end of February. The previous record was 199.09p in June 2022 following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The increase means the cost of filling an average family car with diesel is now £110, £31 more than at the start of the conflict.

Petrol prices are now 41p per litre more than at the start of the conflict, but still well below a 2022 peak.

The RAC data is based on the average price of diesel at a range of supermarkets, motorway service stations and independent retailers.

Simon Williams, the RAC's head of policy, said record diesel prices "spell pain not only at the pumps for drivers, but for everyone who buys goods or services that rely on diesel lorries and vans".

"Undoubtedly these increased costs will be passed on to consumers," he said. Williams said prices at the pumps will not come down until there is a "sustained lower oil price - over several weeks, not days".

The price of Brent crude, a benchmark for global oil used to make petrol, diesel and other fuel products, rose over the weekend and is now hovering at around $108 per barrel. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.

Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets.

Russia, which is also a major producer, has also implemented an export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply.

Diesel is harder to refine than gasoline and, because it is used by the haulage industry and in agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

The UK is heavily reliant on imports. Although the four refineries in the UK make more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel for the country's needs.

There were 15.1 million diesel vehicles on UK roads at the end of June, according to the Department for Transport. That is a drop from 15.7 million a year before.

There were 9.8 million diesel cars, down year on year from 10.4 million.

articles.title: Bin lorry fire in Wokingham prompts vape disposal warning
articles.summary: Crews spotted the fire in the back of their bin lorry after collecting rubbish in Wokingham.
articles.body:
A bin lorry fire believed to have been sparked by a discarded vape has prompted a warning not to dispose of battery-powered items in household rubbish.

Wokingham Borough Council said the fire was spotted by the waste collection crew, who drove the lorry back to the depot and called Royal Berkshire Fire and Rescue Service.

The crew dumped the load of smouldering rubbish while firefighters put the fire out. A thermal imaging camera was then used to check for hotspots.

The council said no-one was hurt in the fire, which happened on Tuesday, but urged residents not to put batteries or battery-powered items in their bins.

It said batteries should instead be taken to a recycling centre or retailer with suitable recycling facilities.

articles.title: Meet Shereen Pavlides, the former Glen Mills resident who turned home cooking into a digital career; the 1990 high school graduate now has about 5 million TikTok followers, 2 million on Facebook and 1.45 million YouTube subscribers
articles.summary: Shereen Pavlides did not plan to become a social media star.
articles.body: Shereen Pavlides did not plan to become a social media star. The Garnet Valley High School Class of 1990 graduate and former Glen Mills resident built her career around food over several years, moving from restaurant work and private mortgage insurance to culinary school, food writing and television. Today, millions of people follow her cooking content online.Pavlides is known online as Cooking With Shereen. She has built a following of about 5 million on TikTok, more than 2 million on Facebook, over 1 million on Instagram and roughly 1.45 million YouTube subscribers. Her online audience grew as she shared simple recipes and cooking techniques from her own kitchen.According to Delco Today, Pavlides' journey into food began early. As a teenager, Pavlides worked in restaurants. She later spent years in private mortgage insurance before enrolling in culinary school in New York City. That decision changed the direction of her career and led her into several food-related roles.After culinary school, Pavlides worked in food styling, food writing and recipe development. She also worked in test kitchens, including at Good Housekeeping. Her experience eventually took her to QVC, where she became an on-air guest and appeared in more than 186 live broadcasts demonstrating cookware, bakeware and kitchen appliances.The TikTok video that changed everythingHer television work played an important role in what came next. Viewers regularly asked Pavlides for her recipes, and those requests encouraged her to create content of her own.She launched her YouTube channel in 2019 and began experimenting with TikTok soon after. One of the videos that helped her gain attention was her fifth TikTok video. It was simple tutorial on making chicken cutlets. The video received millions of views and helped establish her he simple, from-scratch cooking style that became synonymous to Pavlides' online content.Pavlides continued developing recipes and filming them in her own kitchen. She also remains involved in editing her videos even as her audience grew.Her work now takes an estimated 60 to 80 hours a week. Even with a large online following, she continues to develop her own recipes and remain involved in the production of her content.Building a career around cookingThe social media career has also taken Pavlides beyond online platforms. She has appeared on major television programmes and published two bestselling cookbooks. She is currently working on a third cookbook. At the same time, Pavlides is planning to expand her production team as her work continues to grow.Her career has moved from working in restaurants and food-related jobs to creating content that reaches millions of people through several platforms. However, the path has not been limited to one type of food media. Her experience in food styling, writing, recipe development, test kitchens and live television has all become part of the career she has built around her online presence.Her advice to content creatorsPavlides has also shared advice for people who want to build their own careers in content creation. Speaking to aspiring creators at a recent Broadcast Pioneers event, she said creators should focus on providing something useful to their audiences.“Don’t make it about yourself. Give something that can help somebody else and be useful in their lives. Quality of your content really matters, because you are building trust,” Pavlides said.She also stresses on the importance of having a direct relationship with an audience and being genuine in the way content is presented.“Talk to your audience, not at them, and be your authentic self,” she said. “Be good at what you’re communicating and let the rest ride,” Pavlides added.What began with a YouTube channel in 2019 and early experiments on TikTok has since become Cooking With Shereen, with a large audience spread across TikTok, Facebook, Instagram and YouTube.You use AI every day. articles.title: Three dead, including child, in Channel crossing attempt
articles.summary: A 10-year-old child and two 30-year-old women were on board the boat - which was carrying 105 people.
articles.body:
A 10-year-old child and two 30-year-old women have died after a small boat that was attempting to cross the English Channel got into difficulty off the northern coast of France, local authorities have said.

Officials responded to a distress call from the boat, which was carrying 105 people, after it departed from the Blériot Plage in Sangatte on Monday morning.

Three passengers were treated on board but were later confirmed dead by an emergency medical team flown out by helicopter, the French Maritime Prefecture of the Channel and the North Sea said.

Pas-de-Calais prefecture said its initial findings suggested the deaths were caused by trampling but an investigation has been launched to determine the exact cause.

Of the 102 other people on board, nine were treated by emergency services upon their arrival in the port of Calais, the prefecture said.

François-Xavier Lauch, prefect of Pas-de-Calais, blamed the incident on smuggling networks, which he said expose vulnerable people, including children, to the deadly risks of crossings.

The prefecture described the boat as a taxi-boat, which requires migrants to wade out onto the water to board.

Three other people died after similar taxi-boat departures last week, French authorities said.

Monday's deaths take the total number of migrants who have died so far this year to 20, according to Pas-de-Calais prefecture. For the same period last year, it said the number was 21.

Thousands of migrants attempt the perilous journey from France to the UK every year. In doing so, they cross one of the most dangerous and busiest shipping lanes in the world.

More people attempt the route in the summer months when the weather is warmer and when seas are calmer.

The UK recorded the highest number of migrant arrivals so far this year on Wednesday - with a total of 781 arriving in 10 small boats, according to Home Office figures.

Two boats also reached UK shores last week without being intercepted by UK authorities , at Folkestone and Samphire Hoe in Kent.

In July last year, France and the UK agreed on a "one in, one out" returns deal , which was designed as a deterrent to stop boats from crossing the Channel.

The deal allows the UK to return some small boat arrivals while agreeing to take in the same number of people from France who are believed to have a legitimate claim to come to Britain.

In August the UK government said it was making progress in tackling small boats, with the percentage who had made the journey in 2026 much lower than for the same period in 2025 but added it needed to "push further and harder in order to eradicate this vile trade".

So far, 2026 has seen 18,609 people successfully make the Channel crossing, which is 42% lower than the same period in 2025 when 32,188 had crossed in small boats.

articles.title: New NHS-style social care system could take decades, Dilnot says
articles.summary: Sir Andrew Dilnot, who proposed reforms 15 years ago, says the cost of such a scheme would be "very substantial".
articles.body:
A new NHS-style social care system for England could take decades to be implemented, economist Sir Andrew Dilnot has told the BBC.

Sir Andrew, who led a commission proposing reform of the system 15 years ago, said Prime Minister Andy Burnham appeared to want social care to be completely free, including residential costs.

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the cost of such a scheme would be "very substantial".

And with Burnham promising to put his plans before voters at the next general election, Sir Andrew said change "is now further away".

Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home.

However, unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use in England, leaving some people facing huge bills.

In an interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg , Burnham suggested his proposals for social care would mean "everyone contributes, everyone is covered" and refused to rule out tax rises to fund such a system.

He promised to set out more details of his vision in his conference speech on Tuesday.

However, he suggested any proposals would not be implemented before the next general election, as he wanted to stick to the commitments in Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which included a promise not to increase national insurance, income tax or VAT.

Labour MP and former minister Darren Jones told Laura Kuenssberg that scrapping the pensions triple lock was an "option that the government should consider alongside others" in order to fund social care reforms.

The triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest - and keeping it in place is also a Labour manifesto pledge.

But Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, said scrapping the triple lock would not be enough to pay for social care and tax rises would also probably be needed.

The next general election is not due until August 2029, although Burnham could choose to call one earlier.

Sir Andrew told the BBC change on social care "is now further away" than had been implied when Burnham first promised a new national care service for England in a speech in July, shortly after he became prime minister.

He pointed out that if proposals are included in Labour's 2029 election manifesto, that would be 30 years after Sir Tony Blair launched a royal commission on social care and more than 15 years since his own commission reported back.

Social care reform could mean big risks and big rewards for Burnham

Why the PM could finally drop the triple lock pension pledge

By promising an NHS-style system for social care, Sir Andrew said the PM was implying it would be "entirely free".

In England and Northern Ireland, people with assets worth more than £23,250 - including their home - are not currently entitled to help with care costs from their council.

In Wales, social care is also means-tested.

In Scotland, state-funded personal care is offered to all adults who are assessed as needing help with tasks including eating and bathing.

However, this does not include accommodation, food and everyday living costs, which are subject to means testing.

Sir Andrew said a Scottish-style system would still leave people in residential care facing "very substantial bills", which Burnham has said he wants to avoid.

The Health Foundation has estimated a universal social care system in England, with the government funding all support, could cost around £18.5bn a year.

On Sunday, Burnham said he believed the costs would be lower than this but he has not set out how he would fund his plans.

Sir Andrew said he believed an NHS-style social care system could costs "well in excess of £18bn", although a Scottish model could cost half this figure.

He added: "I also think that there was an indication in what [Burnham] said that he's imagining something that could take many years, even many decades before it came to fruition."

Sir Andrew said he would "love to see such a scheme", where all social care is government-funded, but "the cost would become very, very large".

He added that a system where the amount people must pay towards their care is capped, "could still work well for elderly people".

Sir Andrew's own commission proposed a lifetime cap of £35,000.

The report's recommendations were accepted by the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, led by David Cameron.

However, the implementation of the cap was delayed to 2020, with Cameron blaming pressure on the public finances, and the idea was eventually dropped by subsequent Conservative governments.

Other proposals to reform the system have also failed, with Theresa May's Conservative government scrapping plans to make people receiving care at home pay the full costs if they were worth at least £100,000, after this was branded a "dementia tax" by opponents.

Meanwhile, when he was health secretary in Gordon Brown's government, Burnham's plan for a national care service suggested this could be paid for through a compulsory contribution from people's estates after they die.

The idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents and the proposals went no further after the party lost the 2010 general election.

articles.body: Indian-origin Republican leader Nikki Haley's son Nalin Haley, who often makes waves by his anti-immigration stance, has been back with his new rant against H-1Bs. articles.title: Water-starved for 25 years, Tulshi shows its anger through 'Village for Sale' poster
articles.summary: TULSHI/SOLAPUR: ‘Village for sale’, says the poster in Tulshi village in Solapur district.
articles.body: TULSHI/SOLAPUR: ‘Village for sale’, says the poster in Tulshi village in Solapur district. The startling, bold words express anger, sarcasm and a deep disquiet among residents waiting for decades for irrigated water.Sarpanch Sharad More said, “Anyone wanting to buy our village can step forward. For outsiders, the poster is funny, but it reflects how govt has been fooling us for 25 years.”Tulshi is a mere nine km from Sina-Madha lift irrigation scheme, but gets none of its benefits. Residents said they have been left out of the canal network that draws water from Ujani dam and supplies it to several neighbouring villages.The scheme became operational in 2000. Other villages cultivate water-intensive cash crops like sugar cane, vegetables and fruit plantations, including grapes and pomegranates, but Tulshi waits for uncertain rainfall.The village is the last settlement in Madha tehsil. Residents said its saucer-like terrain, surrounded by higher ground, makes it particularly difficult to hold water without a dedicated canal or a pipeline network.The crisis is acute this year. According to the district record, several villages in Madha, including Tulshi, have received no rainfall in the last 45 days. Tulshi’s water bodies have little or no water, while wells and percolation lakes have dried up.“We have been getting tankers since July. That is a reflection of our situation here,” More said.For generations of farmers, the Sina-Madha project has promised to transform agriculture. But villagers said these assurances remain unfulfilled despite politicians’ interventions. “This year, the situation is so grim that we are forced to protest,” villager Pramod Vasekar said.The grim situation led to an indefinite fast by villagers on Ganesh Chaturthi. They submitted a memorandum to the tehsildar warning of collective self-immolation if their water demand was not met.They also threatened to boycott elections. The protest was called off on Friday after water resources minister Radhakrishna Vikhe Patil spoke to them.Solapur district collector S Karthikeyan said the irrigation department has conducted a hydrological survey of Tulshi and examined scientific and technical parameters.“Based on their findings, we will send a proposal to the state govt for a canal network to Tulshi and three other villages,” he told TOI.A senior irrigation official from Krishna Valley Development Corporation said a technical analysis of Tulshi, Bavi, Paritewadi and Anjangaon Khurd was conducted in 2023. “The project cost was around Rs 46.49 crore then, which will escalate now,” he added.Of the 14 water bodies across the four villages, six can be filled through closed pipelines, while the remaining eight would require pumps.“After govt’s approval, work on the ground will take some years. These villages require the pipeline. Otherwise, their struggle for water is not going to end for years,” the irrigation official added.For Tulshi’s farmers, the crisis is visible in their fields. Farmers have abandoned fruit plantations and stopped planning fresh cultivation. Nearly 2,700 hectares of agricultural land may turn barren once the monsoon retreats.An emotional Pandurang Mali said, “It kills me every day to see my crop wither. I can’t water them. I tried to hire tankers, but I can’t afford them now.”Mali, 47, once cultivated about 1,000 pomegranate trees on two acres. His house stands on the now-abandoned plantation. “I poured my sweat and blood into this plantation. Last year, I earned Rs 6 lakh, but nothing this year. I don’t know how I am going to live,” he said.His plantation is barely 100m from one of the village’s water bodies. “If we get canal water, we don’t need any govt help. We will be self-reliant,” Mali said.Farmers turned to dairy farming a few years ago. Almost every family owns cows or buffaloes, but they too are reeling under the water and fodder crisis. “We will have to buy fodder at high prices because of the shortage,” Vasekar said.The village’s social fabric is also wearing thin. “Men are unmarried because nobody wants to give them their daughters. Families reject proposals because of the water crisis. Govt needs to understand all this,” Mali said.The villagers said that employment, household finances, livestock, migration, and the younger generation have also been affected. “And therefore, we feel we should sell our village,” More said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in PuneStay updated with the latest Pune news. articles.title: Passports needed for ferry passengers travelling between UK and Ireland
articles.summary: Previously, passengers were able to use other forms of ID, such as driving licences and national identity cards.
articles.body:
Passengers travelling on ferries between the UK and the Republic of Ireland will need to show their passport from Monday.

Ferry operator Irish Ferries said the new requirement applies to their Dublin to Holyhead and Rosslare to Pembroke routes, in both directions.

Stena Line said all passengers travelling from Dublin, Holyhead, Fishguard or Rosslare ports would also be required to present a valid passport at check-in.

Previously, passengers were able to use other forms of ID, such as driving licences and national identity cards - but the changes are being brought in to comply with UK Border Force rules.

In a statement on its website, Stena Line said the change would meet UK Border Force requirements "in relation to the accuracy and integrity of passenger data before boarding".

Irish Ferries said the requirement would apply to all passengers, including Irish and UK citizens, adding that from Monday, driving licences, national identity cards and other forms of photographic identification would no longer be accepted on the two routes in question.

Irish Ferries said passengers who were not British or Irish citizens and were visiting for a short stay of up to six months in the UK may need an Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA), which allows travel to the UK, Jersey, Guernsey or the Isle of Man for up to six months.

Passport cards will also be accepted by both operators.

articles.title: Mexico's Pacific coast braces for Hurricane Polo
articles.summary: The category-three storm is approaching the state of Baja California Sur, on Mexico's northern Pacific coast.
articles.body:
People living on the northern Pacific coast of Mexico are bracing for the arrival of Hurricane Polo, which is forecast to make landfall later on Monday or early on Tuesday.

The category three storm, with maximum sustained winds near 115 mph (185 km/h), is expected to move over the state of Baja California Sur, a region popular with tourists and home to the resort destination of Los Cabos.

Meteorologists at the US-based National Hurricane Center (NHC) have warned of heavy rainfall which could lead to life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain.

Residents on Sunday stocked up on essentials such as drinking water and food as the storm approached.

The NHC warned of the storm surge Hurricane Polo could unleash, which it said could be accompanied by large and destructive waves.

In Cabo San Lucas, famous for its natural rock arch, the authorities restricted access to the beaches. Some restaurants also closed in the town, which acts as a base for sport fishers and whale watchers.

The regional government of Baja California Sur has ordered schools to remain closed on Monday as a preventive measure.

Governor Víctor Manuel Castro Cosío said temporary shelters had been opened should residents need to be evacuated.

The federal authorities have also deployed thousands of members of the navy and the army along with specialised machinery.

Polo has been slowly moving towards Mexico's coast line.

Meteorologists said it was being fuelled by extremely warm waters caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon.

articles.title: Lithium-ion battery fire killed Bootle mum and three children
articles.summary: Elisha Brabin, 36, and three of her children, died after a blaze at their home in Bootle, Merseyside.
articles.body:
A fatal house fire that killed a mother and her three children was caused by a lithium-ion battery.

Elisha Brabin, 36, and her children, Leo, 16, Ellis, eight, and Prudence, seven, died after a blaze "spread rapidly" inside a house on Stone Square in Bootle, Merseyside, in the early hours of 22 September.

Following an investigation with Merseyside Police, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service (MFRS) said the fire was caused by an electrical event linked to a lithium-ion battery, which are used in e-bikes and e-scooters.

Kev Johnson, of MFRS, said: "This tragedy highlights the very real risks posed by lithium-ion batteries, which we confirmed as the source of the fire."

MFRS said four people "showing no signs of life" had been found in an upstairs bedroom.

A man was taken to hospital suffering from burns.

"This is a devastating incident, and our thoughts are very much with the family and friends of the mother and children who lost their lives and those who were injured," Johnson said.

He commended the efforts of staff and NWAS colleagues "who made every effort to provide a different outcome".

"Sadly this was not the case due to the speed and intensity of the fire," he said.

MFRS has not confirmed what the battery was being used for, but they are often found in e-bikes and e-scooters.

The fire service said there had been 150 fires linked to lithium-ion batteries on Merseyside between April 2023 and August 2026, and five fatalities linked to the batteries.

Johnson said: "We're urging people to follow the manufacturer's instructions - only using batteries and chargers which have been supplied with the vehicle or approved by the manufacturer, as anything else can pose a huge fire risk.

"It's also important to know and recognise the signs that your lithium-ion battery may be failing – if it is swelling, making unusual sounds, has a strong smell, is failing to charge, or is smoking, please stop using immediately."

They said the family had been left "heartbroken" and their "unimaginable" loss would be "felt forever".

They also said "our beautiful babies, Leo, Ellis and Prudence, were loved beyond measure" and they were "devastated by the loss of Elisha, Leo, Ellis and Prudence".

"They have all been taken from us far too soon," they added.

articles.summary: At least 10 people have died and one remains missing after landslides triggered by continuous rainfall struck Nepal’s Baglung district over the weekend,
articles.body: At least 10 people have died and one remains missing after landslides triggered by continuous rainfall struck Nepal’s Baglung district over the weekend, burying homes and sweeping away several houses.A video of the incident shows a section of a mountain collapsing and rushing down the slope within seconds.Nine people died and one person was reported missing in landslides across Baglung on Sunday, while one person was killed in a separate incident on Saturday, according to local authorities.Superintendent of Police Phanindra Prasai, chief of the District Police Office in Baglung, said four deaths and one missing case were reported in Tamankhola Rural Municipality, while five people died in Nisikhola Rural Municipality on Sunday.In Tamankhola Rural Municipality-3, Dharnasuk, 80-year-old Buddhiraj Gharti and 66-year-old Bhimdevi Gharti were killed when a landslide buried their home. Eight houses were swept away in the village.In Tamankhola Rural Municipality-4, Santar, 50-year-old Hastabir Sripali and 65-year-old Udisara Sripali died after their house was buried. Hastabir’s wife remains missing.Four members of a family died after a landslide buried their home in Haddhara, Jugjakhola, in Nisikhola Rural Municipality-3. The deceased were identified as 36-year-old Shyamkumari BK, her 13-year-old son Manoj, eight-year-old son Mukesh and three-year-old son Nishan BK.In Nisikhola Rural Municipality-6, Rangil, 50-year-old Suryabahadur Gharti died after a landslide buried a cowshed.On Saturday, 59-year-old Manbahadur Roka was killed when a landslide buried a house in Dhasmar, Tarakhola Rural Municipality-5.Rescue operations under wayBaglung chief district officer Krishna Prasad Acharya said early warnings helped prevent further casualties.A team of security personnel, supported by a Nepali Army helicopter, reached the affected areas to carry out rescue operations.The landslides in Baglung are part of a wider spell of severe weather across Nepal. At least 21 people have been killed, five remain missing and five others have been injured after four days of heavy rainfall, floods and landslides, according to an update from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).Landslides accounted for 14 deaths and all five missing persons, while floods caused four deaths and continuous heavy rainfall claimed three lives, the authority said.The severe weather affected 247 families, completely destroying 260 homes and partially damaging 80 others. A low-pressure system originating in the Bay of Bengal brought heavy rainfall across several parts of Nepal between September 24 and 27.Emergency teams have relocated around 3,000 people from high-risk areas, while rescue personnel and local authorities are providing food and relief to displaced families. Helicopters have also been used to evacuate people trapped in hard-hit districts.NDRRMA monitoring stations recorded more than 100 mm of rainfall at 106 locations during the four-day period. Dumkuali in Nawalparasi recorded the highest rainfall at 455.2 mm, followed by Pokhara in Kaski at 407.2 mm and Anbu Khaireni in Tanahun at 373.2 mm.The authority has also warned residents living along the Narayani River after it crossed the warning level and entered settlements. articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's covert visit to the UAE focused on denying reports of a pre-October 7 warning from Sheikh Mohamed about a Hamas attack. This meeting raises questions about security failures ahead of the escalating conflict in Gaza.
articles.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu made a secret trip to the United Arab Emirates on Sunday and met President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, with the talks focused on a report that the UAE leader had warned Netanyahu about a looming Hamas attack before October 7, 2023.The hour-long meeting was confirmed by two people briefed on Netanyahu's visit, the Associated Press reported. articles.title: 5 British nationals arrested on suspicion of terror offenses near base U.S. used to strike Iran
articles.summary: LONDON — Police have arrested five British nationals in connection with a massive security operation near a base the U.S.
articles.body: LONDON — Police have arrested five British nationals in connection with a massive security operation near a base the U.S. Air Force used to facilitate strikes on Iran, the counterterrorism officials running the operation said Monday. The men, all from London, were arrested on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses after three suspicious vehicles were seen moving toward RAF Fairford, which is about 90 minutes west of London. Dozens of homes were evacuated and a large emergency presence was seen around the installation, shaking the normally quiet rural area in rural Cotswolds. “This is a hugely complex and large-scale operation, involving local and national policing, the [Ministry of Defense], and local agencies, who are working together to progress the investigation and support for the community,” said Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, the Metropolitan Police’s counterterrorism policing senior national coordinator. Nobody has been charged. Earlier, a local farmer recounted how she had seen a group of hooded and masked men early Sunday. “When they saw me they ran ahead of me — some into the field and some towards the neighboring village,” the farmer, speaking on condition of anonymity, told the BBC News on Monday. “I then realized that something highly unusual was taking place.” Asked if British authorities knew of the threat ahead of time or only became aware after being called by a concerned farmer as has been reported, Defense Minister Wes Streeting told broadcaster Sky News on Monday that the member of the public “did the right thing” and acted quickly. A grainy image has also emerged appearing to show the suspects. The photo, which began circulating on social media Sunday morning, shows five men sitting on the ground shirtless and apparently handcuffed. They are flanked by armed officers. The image geolocated to near RAF Fairford by NBC News. NBC News could not locate the original source of the photo. The suspects, who are all in their early to mid-twenties, remain in custody, Evans said, as investigators probe a possible motive. Their names have not been released. Another image showing three white vans near the air base has also circulated online. Fuel2U, a U.K. fuel delivery company, said in a statement that a version of its logo appeared on one of the vehicles, adding that neither the vehicle nor any of the individuals involved has any connection to it. “We are extremely concerned that our company’s name has been used without our knowledge or permission,” the statement said. After the operation prompted questions about a possible link to Iran, the country’s embassy in London denied the country was involved. “The embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base,” it said in a statement on X. In March, then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer gave permission for the U.S. to use its bases for “specific and limited defensive” operations against Iran. In July, Iran’s ⁠Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned Britain that “any base used to facilitate aggression against Iranian territory is considered a legitimate target,” Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim news agency reported, specifically citing bomber aircraft flights taking off from Fairford. “I am very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised,” Evans said, adding that investigators should be “given the space to work carefully and clearly.” Tristan Wilkinson, a member of the local council, told NBC News that a threat to the base from Iran earlier this summer had heightened the alert level in the community and led to a ramped-up police presence and increased security patrols. Asked about a possible connection to Iran on Sunday, President Donald Trump told reporters: “We know all about them, and you’ll be hearing about it very soon. We caught them.” Trump said in separate comments Sunday that the arrests were an “amazing job.” “They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great,” he said. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them.” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham urged people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts.

articles.title: Hull Maritime Museum wins award for £20m renovation
articles.summary: Judges say the new-look Hull Maritime Museum is "part of a wider programme of civic regeneration".
articles.body:
A museum celebrating a city's seafaring history has won an award following a major renovation.

Hull Maritime Museum was named Refurbishment/Renovation Of The Year at the Insider Yorkshire Property Awards 2026.

The site reopened in August following £20m of work.

Mike Ross, the leader of Hull City Council, said: "The project has breathed new life into one of Hull's most important historic buildings, ensuring its future while creating an outstanding visitor experience that celebrates our city's world-famous maritime heritage."

The Grade II* listed landmark was built in 1871 and was the city's former Dock Offices.

It underwent the renovation as part of the Hull Maritime Project, which was funded by Hull City Council and the National Lottery Heritage Fund.

Insider Media said the refurbishment had overcome a number of issues including "deterioration within the roof structure and asbestos, including aerosol contamination within a lift shaft".

The judging panel praised the "attention to detail" in the renovated building as "exceptional".

"The building's use now has a much wider purpose than it once did and is all part of a wider programme of civic regeneration," they added.

Ross said: "The success of the museum reflects the dedication, skill and passion of everyone involved in the project and demonstrates the value of investing in our heritage assets.

"We are incredibly proud that Hull Maritime Museum is being recognised as the very best refurbishment and restoration projects in Yorkshire.

"The thousands of visitors since it reopened have recognised the quality of the museum, so it is pleasing to see it now get the recognition of this award."

articles.title: Why South Korea is demanding an apology from Ukraine over North Korean PoWs
articles.summary: Seoul says Kyiv agreed to a nondisclosure agreement over the prisoners but broke it.
articles.body:
South Korea has demanded an official apology and explanation from Ukraine after accusing Kyiv of disclosing the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul.

Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said in a statement on Sunday that the president’s office expressed “strong regret over Ukraine’s unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement”.

He said Ukraine had repeatedly discussed the prisoners’ transfer with Seoul through various channels and had requested secrecy.

However, Kyiv has said no secrecy agreement existed.

Speaking at the annual United Nations General Assembly last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea after they were caught fighting for Russia in the Kursk region. Ukraine seized large parts of the Russian border region in August 2024 but has since lost most of the territory.

“These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realised he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself, and he was shocked that fate did not let him die,” Zelenskyy said in his speech.

He also condemned North Korea’s deployment of troops to support Moscow, saying: “This is madness too. Why should Koreans give their lives in a war against Ukraine? [North Korean leader] Kim Jong Un uses them like currency, and he gets something in return.”

Zelenskyy said at the time that he would hand the captured soldiers over to Kim if he could facilitate their exchange for Ukrainians held captive in Russia.

However, human rights groups had urged him to send them to South Korea, referring to possible risks of punishment that the soldiers faced.

South Korean media also reported that the two captured soldiers had wanted to defect to Seoul.

Ukraine captured the two North Koreans in January 2025.

They became the first North Korean soldiers to be captured alive since Pyongyang began in 2024 to aid Moscow’s war efforts against Ukraine. North Korea is estimated to have deployed thousands of soldiers to support Russia’s war against Ukraine as part of a mutual defence treaty .

South Korea previously declined to confirm the soldiers’ arrival, citing concerns about their safety and that of their family members still in North Korea.

But Zelenskyy’s decision to announce the transfer surprised South Korea’s government.

In a post on X, President Lee Jae Myung said the issue of repatriating North Korean prisoners of war was a “highly sensitive agenda”.

“From the perspective of those who advertised the repatriation to the whole world with enthusiastic fanfare to show off their achievements – regardless of the impact on inter-Korean relations, the loss of life, or the damage to national interests – they likely not only cannot understand our government’s efforts to keep it confidential but may even wonder if there is something wrong with it,” Lee wrote.

“I do not know the reasons behind Ukraine’s disclosure in violation of the non-disclosure agreement, but it is deeply regrettable,” he added.

South Korea is technically still at war with North Korea because the two opponents in the 1950-1953 Korean War signed an armistice in 1953 and not a peace treaty. Thousands of US soldiers are stationed in South Korea, and the two allies hold military exercises regularly, which the North has denounced.

According to Seong’s statement on Sunday, Zelenskyy disclosed the repatriation without sufficient prior consultation and later denied that any confidentiality agreement existed.

He added that the denial had seriously damaged trust between the two governments and could harm their relations.

At the same time, opposition politicians have condemned Lee’s government for failing to disclose the transfer.

Last week, opposition politician Ahn Cheol-soo of the People Power Party asked on social media whether it was “fair” that the Korean public learned about North Korean POWs in the country through Zelenskyy.

“President Lee, why did you hide it? Does North Korea have something that, if disclosed, would end your political career? Or were you planning to send the POWs back to North Korea?” Ahn asked.

How many North Korean soldiers are fighting in Ukraine?

According to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, about 14,000 to 15,000 North Korean soldiers were sent to support Russia’s war efforts, and most were deployed to Russia’s Kursk region to fend off a Ukrainian incursion.

As a close Russian ally, Pyongyang has also supplied Moscow with weapons, including artillery and mortar rounds, ballistic missiles, long-range artillery systems and multiple-launch rocket systems, according to Ukrainian and independent assessments.

The soldiers are expected to undergo questioning and security screening before South Korean authorities decide whether to grant them protection and begin resettlement.

On Monday, Seoul’s Ministry of Unification said it would review their cases under relevant laws and past practices, including the North Korean Defectors Protection and Settlement Support Act.

The ministry’s goal is to unify the two Koreas, which were partitioned shortly before the 1950-1953 war. Pyongyang opposes reunification.

Under the law, the National Intelligence Service investigates applicants in temporary protective custody

Yu Yong-weon, an opposition lawmaker who met the soldiers in Ukraine in February 2025, said they served in North Korea’s special forces and could provide information on Pyongyang’s training, military capabilities and participation in the war.

articles.title: Faslane dry docks and research ship to be built in UK, says chancellor
articles.summary: John Healey says orders worth £6bn will be placed with a UK-based shipbuilder as part of a "new age of industrialisation".
articles.body:
Orders for three floating dry docks, worth £6bn, to maintain the Royal Navy's nuclear-powered submarine fleet at Faslane will go to a UK-based shipbuilder, the chancellor has confirmed.

John Healey told the Labour conference the facilities were vital to national security and would support domestic shipbuilding as part of a "new age of industrialisation".

A UK-only bidding competition will decide who builds the floating docks but Navantia UK, which owns sites in Fife and Belfast, is seen as a frontrunner.

Healey has also pledged £115m for construction in the UK of a new marine research vessel to replace Cefas Endeavour, built by the Ferguson shipyard on the Clyde more than 20 years ago.

He told delegates in Liverpool: "I want to confirm today that we, this government will commit to £6bn of contracts for our British shipyards.

"They'll build the new docks for the submarines that will defend us all for decades to come, built in Britain by British workers because of the decisions of this Labour government."

The investment is part of a wider £15bn upgrade of the Faslane site, on the eastern side of Gare Loch, over the coming decade.

Floating dry docks are structures that can be submerged to allow a ship or submarine to enter. They are then raised and emptied of water, enabling inspections, maintenance and repair.

Unlike their land-based equivalents, their ability to float means they can be towed to different locations.

The last floating dry dock to be manufactured in the UK is believed to be Admiralty Dock 60, built in the 1960s and based at HMNB Clyde at Faslane until the late 1990s when it was sold for commercial use.

Currently the base has to rely on a single shiplift, an elevator-type device which hoists submarines out of the water inside a large maintenance building.

The Spanish state-owned shipbuilder Navantia has been lobbying hard to build the new floating docks for Faslane, through its UK division.

The company owns the Harland & Wolff shipyard in Belfast, along with fabrication sites at Arnish on the Isle of Lewis, Methil in Fife and Appledore in Devon.

The GMB union has previously written to Healey asking for the work to be shared between the Methil site and Belfast.

Other possible contenders include the Cammell Laird shipyard in Merseyside, now owned by Balaena, and Babcock which has facilities at Rosyth.

Healey has also confirmed funding for a ship to replace Cefas Endeavour, the UK government's main fisheries and marine science research ship.

Operated by the Centre of Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (Cefas) the ship is based at Lowestoft in Suffolk.

Cefas Endeavour was launched in 2002 by the now nationalised Ferguson shipyard in Port Glasgow on the Clyde, and entered service the following year.

The firm could potentially bid to build the replacement as its size - expected to be up to 85m (279ft) - is well-suited to the yard's capabilities.

But Ferguson's is likely to face competition from other commercial yards such as Navantia and Cammell Laird.

Cefas Endeavour was a technically challenging ship, with exacting specifications for noise and vibration so that it would not disturb fish during survey work.

Still in active service after 20 years, its replacement is expected to be delivered in the early 2030s.

Healey also used his speech to announce that Rolls-Royce will invest an extra £300m into its British factories in Derby, in Bristol, in Glasgow and in Rotherham.

articles.title: JASON CHAFFETZ: Fox News has never let DC scandals become mere footnotes
articles.summary: Fox kept Brian Terry's name on the air after Fast and Furious guns walked into criminal hands and other newsrooms dismissed it as a botched sting.
articles.body: Long after the rest of the media passed on exposing the corruption in D.C., Fox knew when there was a real story. In December 2009, I sat down with Neil Cavuto. It was one of my earliest national interviews. As a freshman who had been in Congress less than a year, I was sleeping on a $45 cot in my closet in Longworth at the time. Cavuto didn’t book me because I had a famous name. He booked me because a member who refused to load pork into an omnibus was news. Fox was willing to bring on a back-bencher from Utah because the story mattered. As a junior member of the House Oversight Committee, I did not know then that this would become the only place some of our hearings got traction after the initial press release died down. Viewers who wanted the whole story knew they could find it on Fox. JASON CHAFFETZ: A DECADE OF SECRET SERVICE FAILURE PROVES THE AGENCY IS STILL IN CRISIS Start with Fast & Furious. The Obama Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives deliberately let guns walk into the hands of criminals so the agency could "build a bigger case." On Dec. 14, 2010, Border Patrol Agent Brian Terry was shot and killed in Arizona. Two of those walked guns were found at the scene. The Justice Department’s first instinct was to minimize it. Other newsrooms were happy to call it a botched sting and move on. Fox kept Agent Terry’s name on the air. We kept asking who authorized a program that ended with an American lawman dead and thousands of firearms unaccounted for. I was not yet chairman. I was a member, but I had been down on that border. Without a network willing to stay on the story, Fast & Furious becomes a footnote and Brian Terry becomes a statistic. Then the Secret Service. By 2015, I was chairman, and the agency charged with protecting the president had become an agency in crisis: a fence jumper with a knife inside the White House, a prostitution scandal in Cartagena, supervisors crashing a crime scene after a night of drinking. We looked into all of it. We held the hearings. Called out the problems. The agency’s response was not to fix the protection mission. It was to open my old job application and pass around "information he might find embarrassing." Forty-five employees accessed my file. A senior official wrote that the information needed to "get out. Just to be fair." This was not a personnel spat. It was a federal agency using private information to punish the committee investigating it. Other outlets covered the fence jumper for a news cycle. Fox stayed on the pattern — and on the retaliation — long enough for an inspector general to put it in writing. 3 SECRET SERVICE OFFICIALS UNDER INTERNAL INVESTIGATION FOR POTENTIAL MISCONDUCT Let’s not forget the IRS. Lois Lerner’s shop slow-walked conservative groups before an election. When Congress asked for the emails, we were told they were gone — hard drive crash, backup tapes that "didn’t exist." It took an inspector general two weeks to find tapes the agency swore were unrecoverable. The White House called the scandal phony. The Justice Department declined to prosecute Lerner’s contempt. A lot of newsrooms took the cue. Fox did not. As chairman I told the country the commissioner had failed to comply with a subpoena, failed to tell the truth about what had been destroyed and failed to notify Congress until after the evidence was gone. You can argue with the politics of that fight. You cannot argue with missing emails and a tax agency picking targets by ideology. That story stays buried if the only cameras left in the room have already declared it over. I’ve been honored to know and interact with so many great Fox personalities over the last two decades. I got to know Charles Krauthammer in the Fox green room, and on the air when he talked about investigations we were running. We did not always agree. I was in awe of his strength. His was a voice I actually listened to, day after day. FOX NEWS DIGITAL HITS 165 MILLION UNIQUE VISITORS IN MAY TO CRUSH BROADCAST NETWORKS, NEWS COMPETITORS One day I said, "Charles, how are you? You’re my favorite person on the planet." He said, "Good to see you, Jason. You’re my favorite person on the Oversight Committee." I said, "My universe is bigger than your universe." He said, "Yeah, well, I’m being generous." Fox News Channel went on the air Oct. 7, 1996. Thirty years later the scandals have different names. The instinct to look away does not. A chairman can issue a subpoena. He cannot make the country watch. For a lot of the years I spent on that committee, Fox was the network that still would. articles.title: Shabana Mahmood to reopen scheme to resettle refugees in the UK
articles.summary: Around 25% of arrivals under the UK Resettlement Scheme are expected to be Afghan women and girls and Palestinians.
articles.body:
Shabana Mahmood will announce the reopening of a scheme to resettle refugees in the UK, as she hopes that offering "safe and legal" routes will deter small boat crossings.

The home secretary will say the UK wants to "live up to our international obligations" by helping those who are fleeing war and persecution, but the process must be "capped and controlled".

The Home Office said the UK Resettlement Scheme (UKRS) will reopen immediately and expects that around 25% of arrivals will be Afghan women and girls and Palestinians.

Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp said Mahmood was making a "desperate attempt to appease" people within Labour who have been critical of her asylum reforms.

Hundreds of people are expected to arrive under the UKRS, which stopped taking new applicants in December 2024, and three new sponsorship routes.

The latter will involve communities, universities and companies hosting refugees from next year.

The Home Office expects arrivals to increase to the "low thousands" as levels of illegal migration fall.

A cap will be set for each year although details of the number have yet to be provided.

People arriving in Britain under the safe and legal routes will be be put on a five-year path to permanent settlement.

Mahmood is expected to tell the Labour Party conference on Monday that "fairness" is behind her approach, limits are needed and communities "must be ready and able to welcome those who come here".

She will also say: "This is what we can do and who we can be as we restore control to our borders, bear down on the small boat crossings, and unlock the inherent generosity of this country."

More than 18,500 people have crossed the Channel in small boats this year compared to more than 32,000 than the same period in 2025.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the UK is "not obligated to take in more migrants", adding if his party was in power then those arriving under Labour's schemes would "not be able to stay".

He said: "If Labour are so sure the public wants their open borders policies, they'd call a general election to get a mandate."

In expressing his criticism, Farage also referenced a report in The Sunday Times about a former bodyguard to the leader of Hamas securing asylum and citizenship in the UK before "plotting" an attack against Jewish people in Europe.

The newspaper reported the man moved to the UK more than a decade ago and now faces extradition to Germany.

Jon Featonby, chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, welcomed the government's new proposals but said it came after a "drastic reduction in safe routes over the last year".

He said: "Safe and legal routes are essential to undermining people smugglers' business model, but they only work if they operate at scale.

"The government has to show ambition and commitment, and that means thousands of places, not hundreds.

"Alongside any new schemes, the government must also reopen refugee family reunion without delay."

Rayner criticises visa rule proposals ahead of Labour conference

UK suspends refugee family reunion applications

Thousands of Afghans were moved to UK in secret scheme after data breach

Safe and legal routes run to bring refugees from other countries to the UK have included schemes helping Afghans following the Taliban takeover of Afghanistan, Ukrainians affected after Russia launched its full-scale invasion and British National (Overseas) passport holders from Hong Kong.

More than 39,000 people arrived under the Afghan Resettlement Programme and in July 2025 the government confirmed the schemes were either closed to new applicants or discontinued.

A scheme allowing refugees to bring their family members to the UK was paused in September 2025.

Government statistics show the UKRS resettled 4,589 refugees after its launch in 2021.

Flora Alexander, executive director of the International Rescue Committee UK, said she welcomed the government prioritising Afghan women and girls and Palestinians under the UKRS.

She described the UKRS as a "well-established safe route" to support people to "rebuild their lives in the UK", adding: "But it needs to be scaled up if it is to make a real difference."

For the Conservatives, Philp said: "We shouldn't be shipping in any more migrants or asylum seekers, no matter how deserving, until illegal immigration has been reduced to close to zero.

"Shabana Mahmood is running scared of Angela Rayner and the Labour left. She is opening up our borders even more in a desperate attempt to appease them."

Rayner, the housing secretary, renewed her criticism of Mahmood's planned changes to the asylum system on the eve of Labour's conference in Liverpool.

The government wants to double the time it takes most migrant workers to qualify for permanent residence from five years to 10 years, while in the case of refugees it could take 20 years.

Rayner warned about shifting "the goalposts years down the line" for people who arrived in the UK at the beginning of this decade, expecting to secure permanent residence under the current rules.

Settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

articles.title: Kill webs, drones and less guesswork: How India's armed forces are using AI in combat
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence is no longer a futuristic idea for India's armed forces.
articles.body: Artificial intelligence is no longer a futuristic idea for India's armed forces. It has already seen combat, even as the services acknowledge that the country is still at an early stage of harnessing it fully. That mix of proven utility and limited maturity defines where Indian military AI stands today.Operation Sindoor offers the clearest evidence. The Army has said 23 AI applications were brought together during the operation, drawing on 26 years of data on Pakistani military movements combined with live feeds for modelling. These tools were about 94% accurate in pinpointing where an enemy gun or missile unit would be located along the border.They also produced a full battlefield picture and post-strike assessments, tightening the Observe, Orient, Decide and Act (OODA) loop that commanders are trained to compress. Among the tools used were an electronic intelligence collation and analysis system, a surveillance network integrated with Project Sanjay, predictive modelling software and an in-house weather application that gave conditions, including wind speed, 48 hours ahead, helping plan extended-range artillery fire.Connecting sensors and shootersThe wider architecture is taking shape around the same idea. Akashteer, the Army's air defence control system, the Artillery Combat Command and Control System and the Air Force's Integrated Air Command and Control System all bring sensors and shooters onto a single interface, so that decisions and orders move faster.Their function is similar to what the Americans attempted with Project Maven. Two bodies, the Defence AI Council (DAIC) and the Defence AI Project Agency (DAIPA), have been set up to steer the modernisation. As India moves towards integrated theatre commands, with wide frontiers, countless sensors and a large mix of weapons, AI is expected to become the connective tissue between them.AI reaches the infantrymanOn the ground, AI is also being built into what an infantryman carries. Israel's SMARTSHOOTER has been recognised in the precision fire control category for its SMASH system, which combines AI, computer vision and tracking algorithms to lock onto a moving target and time the shot, turning a standard rifle into a precision weapon.It is aimed at small drones, and the US Army placed a follow-on order worth about $10.7 million in May. Night fighting is being upgraded as well. Systems such as the AN/PSQ-42 Enhanced Night Vision Goggle-Binocular blend image-intensified and thermal views and overlay navigation waypoints and friendly-force positions, improving the effectiveness of soldiers on the ground.Project Maven and the race to process battlefield dataProject Maven began as the Pentagon's Algorithmic Warfare Cross-Functional Team (AWCFT), tasked with automating the processing of drone video from the fight against the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria.The problem was scale. American forces were collecting terabytes of data every day from hundreds of manned, unmanned and space-based systems, yet much of the footage was never reviewed. The aim was to train software to flag patterns, such as the planting of an improvised explosive device, and warn nearby troops.In March, US Central Command said its forces were using a variety of advanced AI tools in the campaign against Iran to sift vast amounts of data in seconds, while stressing that humans make the final decision on what to strike. It did not name the systems involved.From kill chain to kill webArtificial intelligence is already helping our commanders make faster and better-informed decisions, by turning enormous volumes of data into a usable picture. But speed is only useful if the input can be trusted. India must build its own algorithms, trained on its own data and tuned to its own terrain and threats, rather than depend on systems we cannot fully inspect. We must also remember that an adversary will try to interfere with the data feeding these tools, through deception, jamming or poisoning, so every output needs to be treated with caution. That is why humans must stay in the loop. AI can inform a decision, but accountability for that decision must always rest with a human being, not a machineThis has altered military thinking. For decades, the kill chain was taught as a linear sequence: find, fix, track, target, engage and assess. Militaries tried to shorten their own chain and break the enemy's.AI enables a kill web instead, in which information moves between many sensors and shooters at once. That gives commanders redundancy and the flexibility to strike a target with whichever weapon suits it best, while software sorts incoming data and helps prioritise targets.US Central Command reported that American forces had struck more than 10,000 targets in Iran by late March, and AI is understood to have helped speed up the targeting cycle.Gaza, Ukraine and the limits of machine targetingEarlier Israeli systems were an important step in this direction and a controversial one. Investigations by +972 Magazine and Local Call reported that two tools, Lavender and Gospel, were used in Gaza after the October 2023 attack, with Lavender flagging as many as 37,000 people as suspected militants. The Israeli military disputes parts of that account.Russia and Ukraine have followed a parallel path. Ukraine says several dozen domestically made AI systems are now in use to help drones find and reach targets, and its battlefield detection software is reported to identify roughly 70% of enemy targets across more than a lakh drone video streams every month.Why speed matters on the battlefieldFor the soldier on the ground, the biggest gain is speed. In areas covered by heavy signal jamming, manually piloted drones lose effectiveness, and onboard AI lets cheap drones spot and fly to their targets without constant human control.That shortens the most dangerous phase of any engagement, the gap between a threat appearing and a response being fired, and allows fewer personnel to cover more ground.The technology, though, is not infallible. Current recognition software can struggle to tell a soldier from a civilian or a friendly fighter from a hostile one, and decoys can still fool it when the sensors are not sophisticated enough.For now, AI-assisted targeting works best as an aid to human judgement rather than a substitute for it, particularly in close or ambiguous combat.Giving soldiers a clearer battlefield pictureSituational awareness is closely linked. A soldier today can face gunfire, drone surveillance, electronic warfare, GPS denial and cyber disruption at the same time.AI-assisted data fusion pulls sensor, radar and surveillance feeds into a single picture, which lets a small unit take in far more information than unaided human attention could manage.Beyond AI: Reducing the soldier's physical burdenPhysical endurance also matters. A soldier carrying heavy equipment tires faster, moves slower and is more prone to injury, all of which erode combat effectiveness over a long operation.Passive exoskeletons developed by DRDO with Tata Advanced Systems, along with the JaipurBelt and ArmMax supplied by Rajasthan-based Newndra Innovations to the Army, Air Force and National Disaster Response Force, are meant to ease that burden.Strictly speaking, these devices are mechanical rather than AI-driven, but they form part of the same effort to keep troops effective for longer, especially at high-altitude locations such as Siachen and Ladakh, where thin air and cold already drain stamina.AI and battlefield medicineSurvival after injury is the final piece. Haemorrhage remains the leading cause of preventable death on the battlefield, and most of those who bleed out do so before reaching a medical facility.Decision-support tools such as the American APPRAISE system help medics assess bleeding risk in real time from vital-sign data captured at the point of injury, giving a field medic some of the triage judgement of a trauma specialist.India's Armed Forces Medical Services has also used AI-linked telemedicine for remote casualty triage, letting troops in border areas send vital signs and injury images to base hospitals for real-time guidance.The human still makes the final callThe limits of trust remain the defining constraint. AI systems can be attacked through data poisoning, deception and jamming, and they are still imperfect at separating real threats from decoys.Ukraine officially keeps AI out of the final stage of target interception, even as battlefield pressure pushes towards greater autonomy, because commanders do not yet fully trust machine judgement in high-stakes moments. The United Nations General Assembly has also taken up the implications of military AI for international peace and security.For India and every other force adopting the technology, the direction is clear: AI is speeding up detection, easing physical strain and improving survival, but the decision to fire still rests with a human being.

articles.title: Jharsuguda Municipality faces 75% staff shortage
articles.summary: Jharsuguda Municipality has 60 of 80 sanctioned posts vacant, including all 21 sweeper posts, prompting officials to seek urgent state govt staffing support.
articles.body: Jharsuguda: Jharsuguda Municipality is functioning with just 20 employees against 80 sanctioned posts, leaving 60 positions -- including all 21 sweeper posts and four zamadar positions -- vacant, according to a staff-position statement as of Aug 31.Jharsuguda Municipality vice-chairperson Benugopal Panigrahi on Monday sought urgent intervention from the state govt to fill the 75% vacant posts, saying the manpower shortage was affecting the delivery of civic services, revenue collection, sanitation, administration and execution of development works.Panigrahi has written a letter to housing and urban development minister Krushna Chandra Mahapatra, additional chief secretary Usha Padhee, director of municipal administration Arindam Dakua, Jharsuguda collector Kunal Motiram Chavan, local MLA Tankadhar Tripathy and Bargarh MP Pradip Purohit.According to the letter, among the major vacancies are also 10 of the 15 tax and fee collector posts, seven of 10 junior assistant posts and five senior assistant posts. Both sanctioned junior engineer posts are vacant. Vacancies also exist in posts of head assistant, homeopathy doctor, work sarkar, peon/chowkidar and amin.Panigrahi said Jharsuguda was witnessing rapid urban growth and increasing civic requirements. “The municipality requires immediate filling of all essential vacant posts to ensure timely, efficient and uninterrupted civic services,” Panigrahi said, also highlighting the forthcoming retirement of the municipal engineer on Oct 31. It could further affect the municipality’s technical capacity and supervision of development works, he said.Panigrahi sought deployment of adequate interim manpower until the sanctioned vacancies are filled. “The govt must take responsibility for addressing this critical manpower crisis without further delay and ensure that the required staff are deployed at the earliest,” he said.The staff-position statement also shows that the municipality is using work-charged, contractual and outsourced personnel for some functions, including sanitation, electrical engineering, programme implementation and technical consultancy.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bhubaneswar | Silver Rate in Bhubaneswar | Bank Holidays in Bhubaneswar | Public Holidays in Bhubaneswar | Petrol Price in Bhubaneswar | Diesel Price in Bhubaneswar | CNG Price in Bhubaneswar | LPG Price in BhubaneswarStay updated with the latest Bhubaneswar news. articles.title: Fox News Media's Spotlight Awards celebrate behind-the-scenes stars as network nears 30 years
articles.summary: Suzanne Scott and Jay Wallace celebrated the 2025 FOX News Media Spotlight Award winners at an intimate luncheon hosted by anchor Bill Hemmer.
articles.body: FOX News Media CEO Suzanne Scott and President & Executive Editor Jay Wallace honored the 2025 FOX News Media Spotlight Award winners on Thursday during an intimate luncheon. The FOX News Media Spotlight Awards are an annual tradition for the organization, and management received hundreds of nominations from staff members passionate about celebrating colleagues who earned special recognition. Winners were announced last year at a network-wide town hall, and they gathered at Avra in midtown Manhattan just blocks away from FOX News Media’s headquarters to celebrate alongside their families and colleagues. FOX News anchor Bill Hemmer, who hosted the event, welcomed guests before introducing Scott to the stage. "In a couple of weeks, Fox News Channel will mark 30 years. When we started, we didn’t have a system for recognizing extraordinary people, and there were many," Scott said. "We were just figuring out how to not lose a satellite and keep a guest on the air from remote locations, forget about competing with MSNBC, which had just launched a few months prior, and CNN, which was the national leader in cable news at the time," Scott added. "But a lot has changed since then." FOX NEWS CHANNEL TOPS NBC, ABC AND CBS IN KEY RATINGS MEASURABLE FOR SECOND STRAIGHT SUMMER Scott noted that nowadays, Fox News Channel dominates cable news and regularly competes with and beats the broadcast networks. "We’ve also come up with a way to celebrate our most extraordinary performers," Scott said. The Spotlight Awards launched in 2020, and prizes have since been handed out to staffers on dozens of teams. The annual event gives FOX News media leaders a chance to show appreciation for individuals who show up every day and keep the company on top. Wallace then took the stage to hand out the first award, where he was joined by Executive Vice President Scott Wilder and "FOX & Friends" co-hosts Ainsley Earhardt and Lawrence Jones. Unsung Hero Award The Unsung Hero Award goes to employees who consistently go above and beyond with work that is vital to FOX News Media but often goes unnoticed. This award recognizes those behind-the-scenes stars who keep everything running, often without fanfare, but always with excellence. Director of broadcast contribution Pat Butler "I think Pat preceded maybe everybody in this room because he’s been here since 1995, and he’s got some good stories," Wilder said before sharing Butler’s astonishing role in covering the terror attacks of September 11, 2001. "Pat drove the truck down there on 9/11, he communicated with our assignment desk by dialing an 800-number from a phone booth because cell phones didn’t work, he told them where he was parking the truck," Wilder said. "He shot all of those live shots that morning … he’s been an unsung hero for a very long time." FOX NEWS TOUTED AT ANNUAL UPFRONT PRESENTATION TO ADVERTISERS: ‘WE’RE NOT JUST COMPETING, WE ARE DOMINATING’ FOX Nation producer Tania Joseph "Tania has been with Fox for seven years, working hard and working her way up. She launched ‘The Sean Hannity Show’ podcast and now handles every single episode. She ensures Fox Nation’s content stays at the highest quality. Her recognition is especially well-deserved, because not only does she have an incredible work ethic, she’s also one of the most likable people you’ll ever meet," Wilder said. Field Engineering and Scenic Design Specialist Tiger Stanley "If you’re ever stranded on an island, Tiger is the one you want with you. He’ll have a shelter, a theme park, maybe a bar, and he’ll build it by the end of the day. None of us have any idea how he gets it done … impossible challenges are met all the time. Tiger is there to handle anything," Wilder said. Rising Star Award The Rising Star Award goes to employees who have shown exemplary work ethic and growth during the early stages of their careers. Assignment editor Matthew Donnell "We’re starting with two Assignment Desk staffers from Washington, who have done such good work, that both of them have earned gigs with the politics unit. First, Matthew Donnell, who has begun working as a Political Embed, covering campaigns through the midterm elections," Earhardt said. "Matt always looks for ways to move stories forward, and now he’s going to do it from the field, interviewing candidates, and breaking news in primaries across the country," she added. Associate producer Jessica Sonkin "Second, also from the D.C. desk, associate producer Jessica Sonkin. Jessica was already known for her incredible work ethic, and it was an easy call to make her a political embed," Earhardt said. "Jessica, you and Matt have a lot of long days ahead on the trail, so I hope you’re all caught up on sleep," she continued. "We very much look forward to your dispatches from across the country during this exciting election season." ‘FOX & Friends’ associate producer Carey Gallagher "I personally know firsthand how hard Carey works, never complains, stays under the radar. She produces segments and handles our research packets. We can always count on her to come up with talking points, good intros and important graphics. Like so many of our Rising Stars, she puts in long hours and is always ready to take on more responsibility. Because of that dedication, Carey has earned the trust of both the ‘FOX & Friends’ hosts and the production team," Earhardt said. FOX Nation associate producer Sabrina Baker "Colleagues say Sabrina is exceptionally creative, and reliable. She routinely juggles at least six shows at the same time, and she’s currently leading the production of ‘Park’d’ Season 10. Sabrina adds that she’s excited to keep growing in her role at Fox. We’re excited as well," Earhardt said. MARTHA MACCALLUM: AFTER 22 YEARS, HERE'S WHY I'M GRATEFUL TO CALL FOX HOME Community Service Award This award goes to an employee that has dedicated time and energy to his or her local community and is active in company volunteer efforts. ‘FOX and Friends First’ stage manager Matt Rodriguez "Matt has worked overnights for thirteen years. Despite working the graveyard shift, he still has enough energy to volunteer for his Cub Scouts. He’s a Unit Commissioner for them, and that’s a big job. He works with many different packs of Scouts. And he recently completed the Wood Badge course, which is focused on advanced leadership, so that he can continue to help children grow into the best versions of themselves," Jones said. Washington D.C. assignment manager Lillian Lecroy "She volunteers with American Corporate Partners, a nonprofit that connects veterans with mentors for career guidance. It’s an organization Fox has been proud to support and partner with for more than a decade, and we’re so proud of Lillian for her dedication to the community," Jones said. Innovator of the Year Lead technical director Rich Cozzi "Rich Cozzi is someone I’ve worked with for years, obviously working at Fox, we’re leaner, meaner, better and more experimentative than any other network … he exemplifies this," Wallace said. "I could not be more proud of him … he’s driving automation across all parts FOX News Media, from Business to Weather," Wallace added. "Rich Cozzi, you earned this." "Innovation at Fox means finding better, faster, smarter ways to get the job done," Wallace said. The Impact Award Director Brianne Bombara and recruiter Veronica Baker The Impact Award goes to those who have had some of the most positive overall effects on FOX News Media. This year, a pair of colleagues from the campus recruitment team shared the award for building a first-class recruiting program. "People ask me all the time, I’ve worked for 30 years, and it’s no secret I started entry level, ‘How do you continue to have a successful culture and develop great people?’ That’s because we bring in the best and brightest at the university level, and we design a way to offer the best, top-rated jobs before they leave. These two have done an incredible job, I couldn’t be prouder of you," Scott said. "This year, the team has overseen three intern cycles with nearly 700 participants, made 34 campus visits… they spent 53 days on the road recruiting top talent," Scott continued. "Brianne and Veronica, I’m so proud of this program you have built and, because of your dedication, our internship program is ranked among the best in the country." articles.body: PRAYAGRAJ: At least four persons, including three of a family, died and one other was seriously injured when a two storyed house collaped after a blast in a domestic LPG cylinder at Malwa block under the limits of Malwa police station of Fatehpur district on Monday.Upon being alerted over house collapse incident, joint teams of police and fire department rushed the spot and carried out rescue operations.A senior cop told TOI that there were at least 10 family members in a family living in a two storyed building at Malwa block.He added when a woman member of a family went inside kitchen to prepare food, the domestic cylinder exploded and resulted the collapse of the house.Five of the family members managed to escape from the house while five others were trapped in the debris of collapsed house.The cops however reacued all five trapped persons and brought them at hospital for treatment.Doctors however declared four of them dead and the condition of remaining one was stated to be serious.Stay updated with the latest Prayagraj news.
